{{Short description|Theorem on the behavior of dynamical systems}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Poincaré–Bendixson theorem''' is a statement about the long-term behaviour of [[orbit (dynamics)|orbit]]s of [[continuous dynamical system]]s on the plane, cylinder, or two-sphere.<ref>{{cite book |first1=Earl A. |last1=Coddington |authorlink=Earl A. Coddington |first2=Norman |last2=Levinson |authorlink2=Norman Levinson |chapter=The Poincaré–Bendixson Theory of Two-Dimensional Autonomous Systems |title=Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations |url=https://archive.org/details/theoryofordinary00codd |url-access=registration |location=New York |publisher=McGraw-Hill |year=1955 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/theoryofordinary00codd/page/389 389–403] |isbn=978-0-89874-755-3 }}</ref>

==Theorem==
Given a [[Dynamical system (definition)#Real dynamical system|differentiable real dynamical system]] defined on an [[open set|open]] subset of the plane, every [[non-empty]] [[compact space|compact]] [[ω-limit set|''ω''-limit set]] of an [[orbit (dynamics)|orbit]], which contains only finitely many fixed points, is either<ref>{{cite book| last = Teschl| given = Gerald|authorlink=Gerald Teschl| title = Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems| publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]| place = [[Providence, Rhode Island|Providence]]| year = 2012| isbn= 978-0-8218-8328-0| url = https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/}}</ref>
* a [[Critical point (mathematics)|fixed point]],
* a [[periodic orbit]], or
* a [[connected set]] composed of a finite number of fixed points together with [[homoclinic orbit|homoclinic]] and [[heteroclinic orbit|heteroclinic]] orbits connecting these.

Moreover, there is at most one orbit connecting different fixed points in the same direction. However, there could be countably many homoclinic orbits connecting one fixed point.

== Discussion ==
A weaker version of the theorem was originally conceived by {{harvs|txt|first=Henri|last=Poincaré|authorlink=Henri Poincaré|year=1892}}, although he lacked a complete proof which was later given by {{harvs|txt|first=Ivar |last= Bendixson|authorlink=Ivar Otto Bendixson|year=1901}}. 

Continuous dynamical systems that are defined on two-dimensional manifolds other than the plane (or cylinder or two-sphere), as well as those defined on higher-dimensional manifolds, may exhibit [[ω-limit set|''ω''-limit sets]] that defy the three possible cases under the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem. On a [[torus]], for example, it is possible to have a recurrent non-periodic orbit,<ref name="dheedene">{{cite journal |last=D'Heedene |first=R.N. |date=1961 |title=A third order autonomous differential equation with almost periodic solutions |journal=[[Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications]] |publisher=[[Elsevier]] |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=344–350 |doi=10.1016/0022-247X(61)90059-2 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and three-dimensional systems may have [[strange attractors]]. Nevertheless, it is possible to classify the [[minimal sets]] of continuous dynamical systems on any two-dimensional [[Compact space|compact]] and [[Connected space|connected]] manifold due to a generalization of Arthur J. Schwartz.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schwartz |first=Arthur J. |date=1963 |title=A Generalization of a Poincare-Bendixson Theorem to Closed Two-Dimensional Manifolds |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2373135 |journal=American Journal of Mathematics |volume=85 |issue=3 |pages=453–458 |doi=10.2307/2373135|jstor=2373135 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Katok |first1=Anatole |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511809187/type/book |title=Introduction to the Modern Theory of Dynamical Systems |last2=Hasselblatt |first2=Boris |date=1995-04-28 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-34187-5 |edition=1 |doi=10.1017/cbo9780511809187}}</ref>

==Applications==
One important implication is that a two-dimensional continuous dynamical system cannot give rise to a [[strange attractor]]. If a strange attractor '''C''' did exist in such a system, then it could be enclosed in a closed and bounded subset of the phase space. By making this subset small enough, any nearby stationary points could be excluded. But then the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem says that '''C''' is not a strange attractor at all—it is either a [[limit cycle]] or it converges to a limit cycle. 

The Poincaré–Bendixson theorem does not apply to [[Dynamical system (definition)#Discrete dynamical system|discrete dynamical system]]s, where chaotic behaviour can arise in two- or even one-dimensional systems.
